body_markdown:
Visitors to this year’s Monterey Car Week were likely overwhelmed by the cornucopia of machinery, but among the standouts were a couple of coachbuilt rarities. Styled by Giovanni Michelotti and crafted by Vignale on Lancia chassis, these two cars epitomized the height of 1950s Italian coachwork, and the first of them, Blue Ray I, was singled out for an award by the judges at Pebble Beach.


Both Blue Ray I and II (or, properly in the Italian, Raggio Azzurro I e II) were commissioned in-period by Nardi, a specialist probably best known for its wood-rimmed steering wheels. Thing is, this wasn’t the pair’s first outing in Monterey: More than 30 years ago, they rolled into town just in time for Nardi’s 60th anniversary and were shown at that year’s Concorso Italiano.


Simpson Design


But here’s the curious bit. Not only had these two coachbuilt Nardis appeared at Car Week before, but the last time they arrived, they did so in a sortie of three. And, while Blue Ray I and II were both built using the mechanicals from Lancia Aurelias, Blue Ray III wasn’t even Italian. Underneath, improbably, it was a Mazda 929 sedan.


Simpson Design


Simpson Design


Simpson Design


Perhaps even more improbably, Blue Ray III wasn’t built in a noisy little Turin workshop by a handful of Piedmontese craftsmen who rolled up to work in battered Fiats or on bicycles, but by a young Texan. Specifically, a Texan who already owned both of the other Blue Rays and had in fact spent a number of years just driving Blue Ray II around as a daily.


That man’s name is Jim Simpson. In his current shop, tucked away west of Seattle on Whidbey Island, he’s still very much in the business of both restoring vintage cars into show-worthy condition—and taking Mazdas and elevating them into little jewels.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


## Japanese-Italian Fusion


Ask your average enthusiast to list off a few examples of Italian sports cars, and you’ll likely get the usual answers from Ferrari and Lamborghini, perhaps with an Alfa Romeo or two thrown in. However, from the postwar period into the 1960s, the coachbuilding traditions of firms like Ghia, Pininfarina, and Vignale meant that there were all sorts of one-off or limited-production racing specials running around.


There’s some slight disagreement about who coined the term, but the name for these rare coachbuilt cars among historians of the period is “etceterini,” and it’s exactly what it sounds like. A catch-all category of various makes and models, the rules are basically meant to include any small-displacement artisan-built Italian sports car. Usually running Fiat engines and gearboxes, as most were built near the company’s Turin headquarters, these cars are sometimes obscure, usually very pretty, and almost always special.


And in Simpson’s shop, they’re still being made.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Take this little red coupe, for instance. Called the Italia, it’s got some of the essence of the Ferrari 250 GTO infused into the pint-sized chassis of an original NA Mazda Miata. Looks fun, right? Well, it also happens to be around 60 pounds lighter than a stock MX-5 and is currently running strong with a touch over 160,000 miles on the odometer. It’s one of Simpson’s personal cars, and he just had it out this morning running errands.


This faithful service is exactly why people buy Miatas in the first place: lots of fun, minimal headaches. Clothing that well-judged blend of pragmatism and delight in a style that is Italian-inspired just adds to the fun part. Over the years, Simpson Design has done just that to more than 200 cars.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Inside, the Italia runs a couple of leather bucket seats from Beck, the replica Porsche specialist, and these provide a good opportunity to pause and make note of what Simpson’s vehicles *aren’t* about. The company is not making replicas of existing cars, nor tributes to them. Instead, as a designer, Simpson takes inspiration from the shapes sculpted decades ago, and he reinterprets them into his own work.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


The closest equivalent is the tiny Japanese automaker[Mitsuoka](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/mitsuoka-celebrates-55-years-of-replicas-with-civic-based-oddball/) , which also uses coachbuilding techniques to produce its little oddball cars. Formerly making similarly Euro-inspired fare, its design team has pivoted in recent times to cars resembling vintage U.S. iron, including[a rebodied RAV4](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/mitsuoka-madness-pays-off-buddy-retro-suv-sells-out/) that looks a bit like a K5 Blazer.


Simpson’s process is a bit more traditional in coachbuilding terms. He sketches out the designs and then crafts them in scale form—he’s a longtime scratch modeler, and the shelves of his house are full of tiny Lancias and Alfas and even Lockheeds—to check the design in 3D. Then he hand-shapes the body in steel, and from this, the molds for fiberglass are formed.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Over the years, all manner of variants have been added to the Italia range, some inspired by Zagato bodies, others by Pininfarina Ferraris. They all look like cheeky good fun, and you know they are to drive because they’re Mazda Miatas underneath.


Perhaps the first of Simpson’s creations best exemplifies the spirit of them all. Mazda was so impressed with the Blue Ray III that he built on the chopped-down 929 chassis that the company straight up sent him a then-new NA Miata, and said, “Do something interesting.” Having no other instruction, Simpson settled on taking the sharp-nosed look of the Ferrari Daytona Spyder and applying it to the little Mazda. After all, the most famous example of that car, the one Crockett and Tubbs drove around on *Miami Vice* , was a replica running Corvette gear.


Ferrari rather famously didn’t react well to that replica, but when Simpson brought his “Miami Roadster” down to Monterey, he gave it a test. Parking it at the Concorso Italiano right next to an actual Daytona Spyder, he figured the attending *tifosi* would either be outraged or delighted. Almost immediately, somebody called it cute. It wasn’t a fake Ferrari, it was a little sports car that maybe wanted to be a Ferrari when it grew up.


## Who Throws Their Shoe?


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Currently in Simpson’s Whidbey Island shop, an Italia GTZ is taking shape, getting ready for the owner who commissioned it. However, the custom-car crafting is only a small part of what goes on here, as the business primarily does restoration work. Simpson is a designer, but he was first a master mechanic.


He credits his mechanical proficiency to the tutelage of the two mechanics he was apprenticed to in Texas: Herman Krause and Hasso Schröeder. The former was German and the latter Swedish, and they didn’t take it easy on the young mechanic, insisting he start over from scratch if he missed a single washer on assembling an exhaust. Simpson says that clogs were worn in the shop, and he’d occasionally have one flung at him.


But he also notes gratitude for this tough-love approach; you can’t sharpen steel on butter. It also helped that he loved what he was working on, being fascinated by European sports cars from an early age.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


In his shop are all manner of the delightful oddballs that he owns. A green Saab Sonett was his car in high school, bought when spotted at a gas station. In a side shed is a TVR and an Isuzu 117 and a first-generation 1960s Nissan Silvia. Tucked under various papers and parts is a first-generation Mazda Cosmo.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Next to that is one of Simpson’s own creations, a Swift. Unlike some of his coachbuilt cars, this one rides on a bespoke tube-frame chassis, utilizing just the subframes and 1.8-liter powertrain of an MX-5. As its name suggests, it’s very quick, with 140 horsepower to move its 1400 pounds.


Simpson Design Swift


Simpson Design


Kitty-corner from that is another of Simpson’s personal projects, and this one is the rare exception in that it is meant to be a replica. However, it’s a replica of a car that doesn’t exist—a Speed Racer Mach V. Simpson pops the hood to show the twin-carb setup he’s adapted for the Mazda-sourced four-cylinder engine.


Parked outside are a number of Simpson’s Italia variants and his Miami Roadster, all of them American *etceterini* . Each of them is a joyous little wonder of hand-built craftsmanship and 1960s-inspired design—one of the world’s most beloved roadsters elevated into something even more special.
